content: CD9 antigen is a protein in humans encoded by the CD9 gene. The protein encoded by this gene belongs to the transmembrane 4 superfamily, also referred to as the tetraspanin family. Members of this family are primarily cell-surface proteins characterized by the presence of four hydrophobic domains. These proteins are involved in signal transduction processes that regulate various cellular functions, including development, activation, growth, and motility. CD9 is a cell surface glycoprotein that forms complexes with integrins and other proteins within the transmembrane 4 superfamily. It is present on the surface of exosomes and plays a role in modulating cell adhesion and migration. Additionally, CD9 can trigger platelet activation and aggregation. This protein also appears to facilitate muscle cell fusion and supports the maintenance of myotubes. Furthermore, CD9 is a critical component in the process of egg-sperm fusion during mammalian fertilization. While oocytes are ovulated, those deficient in CD9 fail to properly fuse with sperm during fertilization. CD9 is localized in the microvillar membrane of oocytes and is thought to contribute to maintaining the normal shape of oocyte microvilli. CD9 has been shown to interact with several other proteins, including CD117, CD29, CD46, CD49c, CD81, PTGFRN, and TSPAN4.
